blocks.html: The witnesses reported that this du Tilh was accustomed to swear by the head, body, blood and wounds of our Lord: which is what is commonly called Blaspheming; which is nothing else, according to the exposition of the Theologians and Canonists, than to attribute to God body, members and other things that do not befit him, or else to detract from what belongs to him a. Although in truth Blasphemy ought to be defined otherwise: for, leaving aside the interpretation of the Hebrews and Cabalists, who say that to blaspheme the name of God is nothing else than to express that great and ineffable name, the Tetragrammaton (which ought not to be pronounced or written), by its letters and characters — it must be understood that Blasphemy is a name drawn from the Greek, which signifies detestation, insult, contempt, malediction and vituperation. Whence to Blaspheme, properly speaking, is to despise, detest and treat with contumely God, or his son Jesus Christ b, provoking them with reproaches and insults c. Thus when the Jews threw stones at our Saviour Jesus Christ, they said they were stoning him not for good works (as the Lord justly complained) but for Blasphemy d. And such Blasphemers, by the ancient law, were stoned by the people e; and from that law our civil constitutions, drawn from it, condemn Blasphemers to death: which ought to be religiously observed, and (as Saint Gregory says) without using any mercy f; provided, however, that they are accustomed and hardened in doing so g. Otherwise, for one, two and three times, the law does not put them to death (not wishing to draw too easily to the penalty of death a slip and looseness of language h), but punishes them extraordinarily, according to the quality of the persons and other circumstances observed, the whole being left to the discretion of the judge i: inasmuch as the law thinks that such unaccustomed blasphemies proceed more from some passion, lightness of mind or bad upbringing than from a pernicious will k.

notes.citation: Code 3.43.1 (De aleae lusu et aleatoribus; Justinian's constitution beginning Alearum lusus [vulgate usus] antiqua res est, which says of ruined gamblers ex hac inordinatione blasphemare conantur); the print's Aut. and its title de religioſ. are not explained — C. 3.44, De religiosis et sumptibus funerum, is the adjoining title

notes.citation: John 10 (10:33: "for a good work we stone thee not, but for blasphemy")
notes.gloss: The print's e. is a wrong sort for c.

notes.citation: Novel 77 (Ut non luxurientur homines contra naturam neque iurent per capillos Dei vel similia), the last paragraph, in the Authenticum — printed under the fourth collatio; the standard division places Nov. 77 in the sixth

notes.gloss: Justinian orders that those who swear by the hair or head of God, or the like, and blaspheme, be visited with the ultimate penalties after admonition; the print's bo. is ho. (homines).

notes.citation: Digest 48.4.7.3 (Ad legem Iuliam maiestatis, l. Famosi, Modestinus)

notes.gloss: Nec lubricum linguae ad poenam facile trahendum est — a slip of the tongue is not readily to be drawn to punishment; the same law is cited at annot-019 {e}. The print's maieù. is read as maieſt., a damaged or wrong sort.

notes.citation: The interpreters (commentators) on Code 4.1.2 (De rebus creditis et de iureiurando); Institutes 4.6.11 (De actionibus, § Item si quis postulante, the action on the oath tendered)
notes.original: Les interpretes en la loy. ij. C de reb cre. P. item ſi quis poſtulante. de actio.
notes.gloss: Printed four lines above the marker line; the transcription records only a dot in the key column. The P. stands for the paragraph sign.

notes.citation: Panormitanus (Niccolò de' Tudeschi) on X 5.26 (De maledicis), c. 2 (Statuimus, Gregory IX's decretal on the punishment of blasphemers)
notes.original: Panor' au c. ij. de maled.
notes.gloss: The decretal imposes public penance on blasphemers; Panormitanus there discusses when blasphemy is punished capitally and when at discretion.
